questions.stem: The Balance of Trade (BoT) of a country is defined as:

options.text: Total value of all exports and imports including services and transfers
The difference between a country's merchandise (goods) exports and merchandise imports
The ratio of a country's exports to its GDP
The difference between a country's foreign exchange inflows and outflows

questions.explanation: Balance of Trade (BoT) refers specifically to the difference between the value of a country's merchandise (visible) exports and merchandise imports: BoT = Exports of goods − Imports of goods. A surplus means exports exceed imports; a deficit means imports exceed exports. The broader Balance of Payments (BoP) additionally includes services (invisibles), income, and capital flows.

questions.stem: The World Trade Organization (WTO), established on 1 January 1995, replaced which earlier international body?

options.text: UNCTAD (UN Conference on Trade and Development)
IMF (International Monetary Fund)
GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)
ITO (International Trade Organization)

questions.explanation: The WTO (headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland) replaced GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade), which had been functioning provisionally since 1948. The Uruguay Round (1986–1994) concluded with the Marrakesh Agreement establishing the WTO as a permanent international organization with formal dispute-settlement mechanisms. GATT governed trade through negotiating rounds; the WTO has permanent institutional status.

questions.stem: The theory of Comparative Advantage in international trade was propounded by:

options.text: David Ricardo
Adam Smith
John Maynard Keynes
Paul Samuelson

questions.explanation: David Ricardo articulated Comparative Advantage in 'On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation' (1817). A country should specialise in producing goods it can produce at a relatively lower opportunity cost — even if it has an absolute disadvantage in all goods. Adam Smith proposed Absolute Advantage. Comparative Advantage remains the theoretical foundation of the case for free trade.

questions.stem: India's Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) replaced the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) 1973. In which year was FEMA enacted?

options.text: 1999 (effective June 2000)

questions.explanation: FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act) was enacted in 1999 and came into force from 1 June 2000. It replaced FERA 1973. Key difference: FERA treated forex violations as criminal offences with 'guilty until proven innocent'; FEMA treats them as civil offences. This reflected India's post-1991 liberalised environment and aligned with WTO commitments for easier capital account transactions.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) principle in WTO means:

options.text: A country must give preferential tariffs only to its single closest trading partner
Whatever trade concessions a WTO member grants to any one partner, it must extend the same to ALL other WTO members
Developing countries receive preferential treatment over developed nations
Only the five permanent UN Security Council members qualify for MFN status

questions.explanation: The MFN principle (GATT Article I, WTO cornerstone) is the non-discrimination principle: any trade concession, tariff rate, or advantage extended to any WTO member must equally apply to all other WTO members. This prevents bilateral favouritism and creates a multilateral level playing field. Exceptions include FTAs, regional trade agreements, and the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) for developing countries.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's Current Account Deficit (CAD) primarily reflects a situation where:

options.text: Government expenditure exceeds government revenue in the annual budget
FDI inflows exceed FDI outflows
The total value of imports of goods and services exceeds the total value of exports of goods and services
The capital account shows more outflows than inflows

questions.explanation: Current Account Deficit (CAD) means total spending on foreign goods and services exceeds total receipts from exports of goods and services (plus net income and transfers). India persistently runs a CAD because crude oil and gold imports are very large. It is NOT the same as the fiscal deficit (government budget gap). India's CAD is typically financed by FDI, FPI inflows, and remittances on the Capital & Financial Account.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: 'Dumping' in international trade, which WTO rules allow countries to defend against, is defined as:

options.text: Exporting low-quality or defective goods to developing countries
Selling exported goods at a price below the domestic price or below the cost of production, to capture foreign market share
Importing goods in such excessive quantities that they seriously injure domestic producers
Refusing to pay import duties on goods entering a country

questions.explanation: Dumping (WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement / GATT Article VI) occurs when a company exports a product at a price lower than it charges in its home market or below cost. WTO allows countries to impose anti-dumping duties to offset the margin of dumping. India is among the most frequent initiators of anti-dumping investigations (especially against China). Option C describes a 'safeguard' measure, which addresses a different situation (import surges, not below-cost pricing).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Balance of Payments (BoP) of a country consists of two main accounts. Which combination is correct?

options.text: Current Account (trade in goods, services, income, transfers) and Capital & Financial Account (investments, loans, reserve changes)
Trade Account (goods only) and Invisible Account (services only)
Fiscal Account (government transactions) and Private Account (corporate transactions)
Export Account and Import Account

questions.explanation: The BoP records all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world. It consists of: (1) Current Account — merchandise trade (visible), services (invisible), income (wages, dividends), and current transfers (remittances); (2) Capital & Financial Account — FDI, portfolio investment (FII), external borrowings, and changes in foreign exchange reserves. A BoP crisis (like India 1991) occurs when reserves are critically depleted.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's single largest merchandise import category, which significantly widens its trade deficit in high global price years, is:

options.text: Electronic goods and smartphones from China
Defence equipment from Russia and the USA
Crude petroleum and petroleum products
Coal and other solid fuels

questions.explanation: Crude petroleum consistently accounts for India's largest single import bill — typically 25–30% of total merchandise imports in high oil-price years. India imports about 85% of its crude oil needs. High global oil prices dramatically widen India's trade deficit and Current Account Deficit. Gold is the second-largest import category, followed by electronic goods and machinery. India's dependence on crude oil imports makes it vulnerable to global oil price shocks.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'Terms of Trade' of a country is measured as:

options.text: Ratio of a country's total exports to its GDP
Difference between the value of exports and the value of imports
Ratio of import tariff rates to trading partner's tariff rates
Export price index divided by import price index, multiplied by 100

questions.explanation: Terms of Trade (ToT) = (Export Price Index / Import Price Index) × 100. Improving ToT (index > 100) means a country buys more imports for a given export quantity — favourable. Deteriorating ToT means it must export more to buy the same imports — unfavourable. The Prebisch-Singer thesis argues commodity-exporting developing countries face long-run ToT deterioration. India's ToT improves when oil prices fall (cheaper imports relative to its manufactured/service exports).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'Infant Industry Argument' for trade protection justifies temporary tariffs because:

options.text: Newly established domestic industries need temporary shielding from foreign competition while they develop economies of scale and accumulate experience to become internationally competitive
Industries producing goods for children need permanent tariff protection
Very small companies need subsidies before they can afford to enter the export market
Agricultural infant industries in developing countries should receive permanent MFN exemptions

questions.explanation: The Infant Industry Argument (associated with Alexander Hamilton and Friedrich List) justifies temporary import protection for nascent industries that cannot yet compete with established foreign rivals. Once the industry matures, achieves economies of scale, and builds expertise (learning-by-doing), protection is gradually removed. Critics (free traders) note that 'temporary' protection frequently becomes permanent due to political economy pressures, and protected industries often fail to become competitive.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India were established primarily to:

options.text: Provide exclusive residential zones for foreign nationals working in India
Promote export-led manufacturing and foreign investment through tax incentives, simplified regulations, and world-class infrastructure in designated enclaves
Create separate judicial zones where foreign companies operate under international arbitration law
Store strategic oil, gas, and mineral reserves outside the purview of environmental regulations

questions.explanation: India's SEZ Act 2005 designates geographically defined enclaves treated as 'foreign territory' for customs purposes. SEZ units enjoy: income tax exemptions (for initial years), duty-free capital goods imports, single-window regulatory clearances, and exemption from several state taxes. The goal is to boost exports, attract FDI, and develop manufacturing infrastructure. Notable SEZs include those at GIFT City (Gujarat), Visakhapatnam (AP), and Noida (UP).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Doha Development Round of WTO negotiations (launched November 2001) is described as a 'development round' because:

options.text: It was hosted in a developing country for the first time in WTO history
All official negotiations were conducted in Arabic, the host country's language
It focused exclusively on issues of concern to wealthy OECD nations

It placed the interests of developing and least-developed countries at centre, particularly securing reductions in agricultural subsidies in developed nations and special differential treatment for poor countries

questions.explanation: The Doha Development Agenda specifically aimed to improve trade prospects for developing countries by: (1) reducing farm subsidies in the US, EU, and other developed nations; (2) improving market access for developing-country goods; (3) granting special and differential treatment to LDCs. The round has been largely stalled since the 2008 Geneva breakdown due to deep disagreements on agriculture between the US/EU and major developing economies (India, Brazil, China) — India's food security concerns being a key sticking point.

questions.stem: India's top merchandise export categories historically include which of the following?

options.text: Crude petroleum, coal, and raw iron ore
Aircraft, spacecraft, and military equipment
Petroleum products (refined), gems and jewellery, engineering goods, and pharmaceuticals
Passenger automobiles and consumer electronics (smartphones)

questions.explanation: India's top merchandise export categories: (1) Petroleum products — India is a major refinery hub, importing crude and exporting refined products; (2) Gems and jewellery — India cuts and polishes ~90% of world's diamonds (Surat); (3) Engineering goods — machinery, auto components, equipment; (4) Pharmaceuticals — India is the 'pharmacy of the world', a top generic drug exporter. Textiles, chemicals, and organic chemicals also feature prominently. India does not significantly export crude petroleum or spacecraft.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: A 'managed float' (or 'dirty float') exchange rate regime, which India follows, is best described as:

options.text: Exchange rate adjusts automatically through supply and demand with zero government intervention
Exchange rate is fixed by a committee of WTO members meeting annually
Only developing country central banks may intervene; developed countries must maintain pure floats
Exchange rate is primarily market-determined but the central bank (RBI) intervenes occasionally to smooth excessive volatility or prevent misalignment

questions.explanation: Under a managed (dirty) float, the currency's value is set by market forces (supply and demand) but the central bank reserves the right to intervene by buying or selling foreign exchange to prevent excessive volatility or large misalignments. India's RBI intervenes in the forex market to manage the rupee's exchange rate. This contrasts with: (a) a pure float — no intervention; (b) a fixed peg — central bank maintains a specific rate. Most major economies use managed floats.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's service exports (IT/ITES software, remittances from the diaspora) are important in the Balance of Payments context because they:

options.text: Appear in the Current Account's 'invisibles' section and help offset India's large merchandise trade deficit, reducing the overall Current Account Deficit
Are counted in the merchandise (visible) export figures along with physical goods
Are recorded in the Capital Account and help finance FDI outflows
Are excluded from official BoP calculations because they are intangible

questions.explanation: Services (IT, BPO, software exports) and private remittances are recorded under 'invisibles' in the Current Account. India runs a persistent merchandise trade deficit (goods imports > goods exports), but the large surplus on services and remittances substantially offsets it. India's IT/ITES exports (~$200 billion+ annually) and remittances (~$100 billion+ — world's largest) make it a global services export powerhouse and reduce the overall CAD significantly.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) is used in international economics primarily to:

options.text: Set official currency exchange rates between WTO member countries
Measure consumer price inflation within a single country over time
Compare countries' economic output (GDP) by adjusting for price level differences, making cross-country comparisons more meaningful than using market exchange rates alone
Calculate the price parity between urban and rural areas within a country

questions.explanation: PPP theory compares the 'purchasing power' of currencies in their own countries by asking: how much does a comparable basket of goods cost in each country? PPP-adjusted GDP comparisons reveal that poorer countries' output is underestimated when using market exchange rates because their price levels are lower. On PPP basis, India is the 3rd largest economy globally; on nominal (market exchange rate) GDP, it ranks lower. The World Bank and IMF use PPP for comparative economic analysis and poverty measurement.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's 1991 Balance of Payments crisis, which triggered the LPG economic reforms, was characterised by:

options.text: Excessive FDI outflows causing a capital account crisis
Foreign exchange reserves falling to barely 3 weeks of import cover, forcing India to pledge 47 tonnes of gold to secure emergency loans from the Bank of England and Bank of Japan
A sudden collapse of India's IT export earnings due to a global recession
Nationalisation of private banks causing a foreign confidence crisis

questions.explanation: By mid-1991, India's forex reserves were critically low — approximately $1 billion (barely 2–3 weeks of import cover). The government (under Chandra Shekhar, then Narasimha Rao) airlifted 47 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England and Bank of Japan as collateral to secure emergency loans. Triggered by the Gulf War oil shock and fiscal mismanagement, this crisis provided the political will for Finance Minister Manmohan Singh to launch sweeping LPG reforms — dismantling the Licence Raj, industrial licensing, and trade barriers.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) differs from Foreign Institutional Investment (FII/FPI) primarily in that:

options.text: FDI goes only to developing countries; FII is restricted to developed economies
FDI is allowed only in manufacturing; FII is allowed only in the financial services sector
FDI flows through bilateral trade agreements and requires WTO approval
FDI involves long-term investment with managerial control (typically ≥10% equity stake); FII/FPI is portfolio investment in stocks and bonds, callable quickly without seeking management control

questions.explanation: FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) involves acquiring significant ownership (≥10% equity per IMF definition) in a foreign enterprise with intent to influence management — factories, wholly-owned subsidiaries. It represents long-term commitment. FII/FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment) involves buying stocks, bonds, or other financial instruments without seeking control. FPI is 'hot money': it can exit rapidly in response to economic or political changes, causing exchange rate and stock market volatility. India has historically preferred FDI over FPI for this stability reason.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: India's service exports and remittances partially offset its merchandise trade deficit. However, India's merchandise trade deficit has grown in recent decades partly because:

options.text: India banned all manufactured exports under WTO pressure
Western sanctions have blocked India from most export markets
India voluntarily removed all import tariffs on every product after joining WTO in 1995
India's import bill for crude oil, gold, and electronics has grown faster than export revenues, widening the gap between goods imports and goods exports

questions.explanation: India's persistent merchandise trade deficit is driven by: (1) crude oil — India imports ~85% of its oil needs and the import bill balloons with high global prices; (2) gold — India is the world's second largest gold consumer and imports 700–900 tonnes annually; (3) electronics — smartphones, components, and semiconductors are heavily imported. While export revenues have grown (pharma, IT services, engineering goods), these three import categories have grown faster, widening the merchandise trade gap.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Country X can produce both wheat and textiles efficiently. Country Y can also produce both, but is less efficient overall. An economist still argues they should trade. The correct theoretical basis is:

options.text: Absolute Advantage — Country X must be absolutely better at one good for trade to occur

Comparative Advantage — if Country X's relative efficiency advantage is greater in wheat than in textiles, X should specialise in wheat and Y in textiles; both gain by trading even if X is more efficient at everything
Heckscher-Ohlin theorem — the decision to trade depends solely on factor endowments (land, labour), not relative efficiency
Infant Industry principle — Country Y needs temporary protection to develop textile competitiveness

questions.explanation: Ricardo's Comparative Advantage: even if X can produce both goods more efficiently than Y (absolute advantage in both), it is still mutually beneficial to trade if X's relative efficiency advantage is larger in one good. X's opportunity cost of producing textiles (in terms of foregone wheat) may be higher than Y's. So X specialises in wheat (lower opportunity cost), Y in textiles (lower opportunity cost), and both trade — consuming more than in autarky. This extends Adam Smith by showing trade benefits arise from relative, not absolute, differences.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Heckscher-Ohlin (H-O) theorem of international trade predicts that:

options.text: Countries should export goods that intensively use their relatively abundant factor of production (e.g., labour-abundant countries export labour-intensive goods) and import goods requiring their relatively scarce factor
Trade occurs only when technology differs between countries, not when factor endowments differ
The absolute size of a country's economy (nominal GDP) determines which goods it exports
Countries specialise based on productivity differences regardless of whether those differences arise from natural endowments or technology

questions.explanation: The H-O theorem (Heckscher 1919, Ohlin 1933) explains WHY comparative advantage arises — through factor endowments. A labour-abundant country (like India) should export labour-intensive goods (garments, handicrafts) and a capital-abundant country (like Germany) should export capital-intensive goods (machinery). The Leontief Paradox (1953) challenged H-O by finding that the US — capital-rich — actually exported labour-intensive goods, spurring extensions like the technology gap and human capital models.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: At the WTO, India blocked the Trade Facilitation Agreement in 2014 unless food security concerns were addressed. India's specific demand was:

options.text: Complete abolition of the Agreement on Agriculture for developing nations
Mandatory increase in tariffs on food imports to protect Indian farmers

A permanent 'peace clause' exempting developing countries' government food procurement programmes (like India's MSP-based buying for the PDS) from WTO subsidy limit obligations while a permanent solution was negotiated
Transfer of all WTO agricultural dispute settlements to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)

questions.explanation: India's key WTO demand (Bali 2013, subsequent standoff 2014) was a permanent peace clause from the Agreement on Agriculture's (AoA) subsidy limit rules for government food procurement. WTO's AoA caps food subsidies at 10% of agricultural output for developing countries — India's large-scale MSP-based procurement for the Public Distribution System (Food Security Act 2013) potentially breaches this limit. India argued food security is a fundamental developmental right that WTO trade rules should not constrain.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'J-Curve effect' in international economics refers to which phenomenon that follows a currency depreciation?

options.text: The trade deficit initially worsens (J's downward stroke) before improving over time (J's upward stroke), because import prices rise immediately while export volume adjustment takes longer
Exports grow in a J-shape — slowly at first after trade liberalisation, then exponentially as new markets open
FDI inflows initially fall after liberalisation, then rise sharply once investor confidence is established
GDP contracts during early reform years, then accelerates sharply in a J-shaped trajectory

questions.explanation: The J-Curve effect: after a currency depreciation, the trade balance initially deteriorates before improving, tracing a J shape over time. Immediately after depreciation, import prices (in domestic currency) rise — raising the import bill — while export volumes take time to increase because trade contracts are fixed and foreign buyers need time to switch to now-cheaper domestic goods. After 12–18 months, export volumes rise and import volumes fall, improving the trade balance. The Marshall-Lerner condition states improvement occurs when the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: By BoP accounting identity, a country running a persistent Current Account Deficit must simultaneously be:

options.text: Running a surplus on the trade balance within the Current Account
Running a surplus on the services account within the Current Account
Running a government fiscal surplus to compensate
Attracting a net surplus on its Capital and Financial Account (net capital inflows) and/or running down its foreign exchange reserves to finance the deficit

questions.explanation: By the BoP accounting identity: Current Account + Capital & Financial Account + Change in Reserves = 0. A Current Account Deficit must be financed by a surplus on the Capital & Financial Account (net capital inflows — FDI, FPI, loans, NRI deposits) and/or a drawdown of foreign exchange reserves. If a country cannot attract sufficient capital inflows, it depletes its reserves — the path to a BoP crisis (India 1991). India's CAD is typically financed by FDI and FPI inflows and large remittances on the current account.
